analysis.one_liner: Requires large animal feedlots to get pollution permits, monitor groundwater, and phase out open-air waste lagoons.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on February 12, 1998 and to its Water Resources subcommittee two weeks later, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have treated large livestock and poultry operations — called concentrated animal feeding operations — as regulated polluters under the Clean Water Act. Every covered operation would need a federal permit with water monitoring and recordkeeping, a government-approved waste management plan, and technology standards: unlined waste pits banned within five years, open-air lagoons eliminated within ten, and no discharges to surface or groundwater. It also made companies that own the animals jointly liable for penalties when a feedlot they supply pollutes, and restricted spraying waste near homes and wells.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near large feedlots and drink from or swim in affected waters. The bill cites drinking-water outbreaks and fish kills linked to animal waste, and its rules target the pathogens, nutrients, and runoff that cause them [S3]. Taxpayers and rural communities also gain because operators, not the public, would bear cleanup and monitoring costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Rural residents and communities near feedlots

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any covered feedlot to discharge pollutants except under a permit requiring surface and groundwater monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting [S2][S3].

Requires EPA standards to phase out unlined waste containment structures within five years and eliminate open-air waste lagoons within ten years, and to eliminate discharges to surface and groundwater [S2][S3].

Restricts land application of animal waste to levels crops can actually absorb, bans applying waste to frozen ground or snow, and sets buffer distances for aerial spraying near homes, wells, and waterways [S3].

Makes each owner of animals at a violating feedlot jointly liable for penalties, in proportion to the animals they own, reaching the large corporations that own livestock while contract farmers run the facilities [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large livestock and poultry producers, and the meat companies that own contract-grown animals, who would pay for permits, monitoring, waste management plans, and replacing lagoons and unlined pits with contained systems. Some of that cost would flow to meat prices and to mid-size family operations that cross the bill's thresholds.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large feedlot operators and meat companies

drawbacks.text: The permit, plan, and monitoring requirements apply to operations above modest thresholds — for example 350 mature dairy cattle, 1,000 hogs, or 50,000 birds — which could sweep in well-run family operations and impose significant paperwork and compliance costs on them [S3].

Mandating new containment technology and lagoon replacement carries real capital costs that would largely be passed through to meat prices, and critics of uniform federal permitting argue states already run water permit programs and could tailor rules locally [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case in the bill's own findings is strong: it cites a drinking-water outbreak that killed more than 100 people and fish-killing algae outbreaks linked to animal feeding operations [S3]. The main honest cost is compliance burden on mid-size farms above the thresholds, though the largest operations with open lagoons are precisely those the bill aimed at. On balance the benefits to water quality and drinking water likely outweigh the costs, with the caveat that a less sweeping version could have exempted smaller operations.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: the House referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee the day it was introduced, the committee sent it to its Water Resources and Environment subcommittee two weeks later, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller of California and nine Democratic colleagues introduced the bill on February 12, 1998 [S1][S4][S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day [S5].
On February 26, 1998 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, where it remained with no hearing, markup, or floor action [S5].
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 without the bill ever receiving a vote, so it died [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large livestock and poultry operations and the meat companies that own contract-grown animals are better off, because they never faced the permit, monitoring, and lagoon-phase-out costs the bill would have imposed. Communities near feedlots gained nothing and continued to live with the pollution risks the bill cited.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large feedlot operators and meat integrators

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 12, 1998 and sent it to the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee on February 26, 1998, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors were Democrats and no Republican support or opposition is recorded; the bill never advanced far enough for a vote that would reveal the partisan split.

industries.industry: Large livestock and poultry producers (concentrated animal feeding operations)
industries.note: The bill would have required every operation above set animal thresholds to obtain a permit, monitor groundwater, and follow a government-approved waste management plan, with discharges to water made unlawful [S3]. Its interest in avoiding those compliance costs runs against the public's interest in clean water and safe drinking water.

industries.industry: Meat integrators and animal owners (corporate owners of contract-grown livestock)
industries.note: The bill made each animal owner jointly liable, in proportion to animals owned, for penalties when the feedlot housing their livestock violates discharge rules, reaching companies that own animals while shifting facility management to contract farmers [S3].

industries.industry: Waste containment and manure-management technology suppliers
industries.note: The bill required operators to adopt best available technology, ban unlined structures within five years, and phase out open-air lagoons within ten, creating demand for alternative containment and waste-reduction systems [S2][S3].
